sessions.title: Development conversation 1
sessions.preparation: Bring the abandoned-call figures for the last four weeks and the decision you made in response to each spike.
sessions.notes: Reviewed the Tuesday abandoned-call spike. Sophie described her conversation with the two senior advisers and recognised she had asked for agreement rather than set an expectation. No standard currently exists in writing.
sessions.summary: Abandoned calls reached fourteen per cent on a Tuesday afternoon while two senior advisers extended their after-call work. Sophie described asking both advisers whether they thought the current wrap-up time was reasonable, then accepting their view that the queue would settle on its own. She had framed a standard as an opinion to be agreed, which left the team without a decision to work to. Sophie's promotion from inside the team still shapes how she speaks: eleven months in, she looks for consent before stating what the service requires. Nothing in the queue changed this month, but she can now name the moment she converted a management decision into a request for approval. The two advisers involved are the ones she trained as a peer, so the conversation she is avoiding is with them specifically rather than with the team. She is not yet clear what she would say if an adviser openly disagreed with a standard she had set. She left with one commitment: write down the after-call standard she believes the service needs, in one sentence, before the next team huddle. The next conversation looks at whether she can state that standard aloud without asking the team to ratify it.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Sophie's promotion from inside the team still shapes how she speaks: eleven months in, she looks for consent before stating what the service requires.

The two advisers involved are the ones she trained as a peer, so the conversation she is avoiding is with them specifically rather than with the team.

Her instinct to check the data first is strong; her instinct to act on it in the same week has not formed yet.
sessions.strengthsObserved: Sophie reads operational data quickly and accurately, and brought the abandoned-call trend to this conversation before anyone above her had raised it.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Remember that Sophie hears a standard as a judgement about her former peers. Separating the expectation from the relationship will make the next conversation easier.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Awareness is the change at this stage: Sophie can describe her own consent-seeking pattern, although she has not yet tested anything different in the queue.
sessions.agreedActions: Write down the after-call standard she believes the service needs, in one sentence, before the next team huddle
sessions.suggestedFocus: whether she can state that standard aloud without asking the team to ratify it
sessions.coachReflection: The question is not whether Sophie is confident enough. It is whether she believes a manager is allowed to decide something her former colleagues have not agreed to.

sessions.title: One-to-one
sessions.preparation: Aurelia prompt: think about the exception you granted. What would have to be true for it to end, and who currently knows that?
sessions.notes: Sophie set a fifteen-minute after-call standard at the huddle and softened it for one adviser within days. Discussed the difference between announcing and holding. Agreed to close the open exception with a date.
sessions.summary: Sophie followed up with one adviser the same week and, when he explained a complex complaint case, told him not to worry about the cap for now. Sophie announced a fifteen-minute cap on routine after-call work at the Monday huddle and wrote it on the team board. Sophie holds a standard with a group and loses it with an individual, which suggests the difficulty is relational rather than a lack of clarity. The standard survived in public and dissolved in private, which teaches the team that the board is advisory and the corridor is where decisions are made. Setting the expectation at all is new. A month ago she would have raised the issue as a question to the whole team and left it there. The exception has not been revisited, so the adviser is still working to the old pattern with her implicit permission. She used the phrase 'for now' twice when describing the exception and could not say what would bring it to an end. The agreed step is to go back to the adviser this week and agree a date from which the fifteen-minute cap applies to his work again. Attention now turns to keeping an expectation intact when the person in front of her offers a plausible exception.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Sophie holds a standard with a group and loses it with an individual, which suggests the difficulty is relational rather than a lack of clarity.

She used the phrase 'for now' twice when describing the exception and could not say what would bring it to an end.

Her follow-up came within seven days, which is faster than anything she described last month; the timing is improving before the content does.
sessions.strengthsObserved: She acted on her own commitment within a week and put the expectation somewhere visible rather than relying on people remembering a conversation.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Sophie manages the group well and the individual less well. Prepare her for resistance in the one-to-one rather than for the announcement itself.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: A first experiment rather than established practice: the expectation was set, then softened as soon as a former peer offered a reasonable-sounding case.
sessions.agreedActions: Go back to the adviser this week and agree a date from which the fifteen-minute cap applies to his work again
sessions.suggestedFocus: keeping an expectation intact when the person in front of her offers a plausible exception
sessions.coachReflection: Watch whether Sophie treats the exception as a mistake to regret or as information about where her authority still feels borrowed. The second reading will serve her better.

sessions.title: Feedback conversation
sessions.preparation: Bring the after-call figures for both senior advisers and be ready to say what you will do if one improves and the other does not.
sessions.notes: First direct feedback conversation about after-call work. Sophie led with six weeks of data, held the standard when workload was raised and agreed a weekly review figure. Opened with two apologies.
sessions.summary: Sophie held a one-to-one with the senior adviser whose after-call average had sat nine minutes above the team for six consecutive weeks. She stayed with the evidence when he moved the discussion to workload and fairness, and the conversation ended with an agreed figure rather than an agreed feeling. Sophie opened with the six-week pattern instead of reassurance, described the effect on queue cover between two and four, and asked him what he made of it. She rehearsed this conversation three times and still opened well, so preparation is helping rather than turning into avoidance. This is the first time Sophie has raised a performance pattern with a former peer and finished the conversation with the standard still in place. Evidence gives Sophie somewhere to stand. Describing numbers she is direct; describing her own expectations she becomes tentative. She apologised twice during the opening, softening a message that did not need softening. The following session will test removing the apology from the opening so the message arrives without being discounted in advance. Sophie committed to give the adviser his weekly after-call average at every one-to-one, whether the figure improves or not.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Evidence gives Sophie somewhere to stand. Describing numbers she is direct; describing her own expectations she becomes tentative.

The adviser accepted the figure without argument, which suggests the resistance she had anticipated was largely her own.

She rehearsed this conversation three times and still opened well, so preparation is helping rather than turning into avoidance.
sessions.strengthsObserved: Sophie held the evidence steady under pressure to renegotiate it, and named a specific queue consequence instead of a general concern about performance.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Preparation is working for her. The next constraint is the apologising, which is habitual rather than chosen and will not respond to more preparation.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Behavioural change now, not only awareness: a difficult conversation was carried to a conclusion with a measurable commitment attached.
sessions.agreedActions: Give the adviser his weekly after-call average at every one-to-one, whether the figure improves or not
sessions.suggestedFocus: removing the apology from the opening so the message arrives without being discounted in advance
sessions.coachReflection: Sophie's difficulty was never courage. It was permission. Notice how much steadier she becomes when the standard belongs to the service rather than to her.

sessions.title: Performance conversation
sessions.preparation: Bring the allocation trial: what the adviser decided, what you would have decided, and what difference it made to the service level.
sessions.notes: Reviewed the four-week allocation trial. Sophie set the target and constraints, left the first allocation uncorrected and reduced her checking through the week. Morning time currently unallocated.
sessions.summary: Daily queue allocation, which Sophie had done herself every morning since taking the role, moved to a senior adviser for a four-week trial. She gave him the service-level target, the two constraints that genuinely matter and no method at all, then left his first day's allocation alone even though she would have split the afternoon differently. The trial is not really about allocation. It is about whether Sophie can let a decision be made differently from her own way and still own the result. Sophie has delegated the task and kept the anxiety, checking the outcome more often than the adviser needs her to. She checked the allocation twice on the first day and once by the fourth, and intervened on neither. The senior adviser she chose is the one she found hardest to give feedback to last month, which is a deliberate and shrewd choice. Her mornings are now free and she has not decided what that time is for, so the risk is that the queue quietly fills it again. She left with one commitment: decide what the freed morning hour is for and protect it for adviser one-to-ones and quality reviews. The next conversation looks at whether the allocation holds on a day when the service level is missed and taking it back feels obvious.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Sophie has delegated the task and kept the anxiety, checking the outcome more often than the adviser needs her to.

The senior adviser she chose is the one she found hardest to give feedback to last month, which is a deliberate and shrewd choice.

Team ownership is starting to show in small ways: two advisers proposed swapping breaks to cover the two-to-four dip without being asked.
sessions.strengthsObserved: She handed over a live decision with clear boundaries and no prescribed method, which is the harder and more developmental form of delegation.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Sophie needs somewhere useful to put her attention. Without a defined purpose for the freed morning, this delegation will reverse itself.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Ownership is moving outward: a daily operational decision now sits with an adviser, and the team has begun proposing fixes unprompted.
sessions.agreedActions: Decide what the freed morning hour is for and protect it for adviser one-to-ones and quality reviews
sessions.suggestedFocus: whether the allocation holds on a day when the service level is missed and taking it back feels obvious
sessions.coachReflection: The useful test is not whether this trial succeeds. It is what Sophie does on the first day it goes wrong in front of the team.

sessions.title: Development review
sessions.preparation: Aurelia prompt: what would an observer see this team doing now that they would not have seen in February, and who is doing it?
sessions.notes: Huddle run as an open question on the afternoon dip. Four suggestions captured, each given a named owner and a review date. Ownership concentrated in two experienced advisers.
sessions.summary: Sophie asked the advisers what they would change, wrote the four suggestions on the board, and closed the huddle by naming an owner and a review date for each one. A team huddle about the two-to-four abandoned-call dip, run as an open question rather than a briefing. The advisers' suggestions were more operationally specific than her own, which Sophie noticed aloud and did not treat as a threat. Naming owners at the end is what turned a good discussion into a set of commitments, and it is exactly the part she would once have left implicit. Six months ago she brought solutions to the huddle and asked for agreement. She now brings the problem and holds people to what they propose. Two of the four owners are the same experienced advisers, so ownership is spreading across ideas but not yet across people. Accountability now runs through a mechanism — owner, action, date — rather than depending on whether she feels able to chase someone. The agreed step is to allocate the next two improvement items to advisers who have not owned anything yet, briefing them privately first. Attention now turns to spreading ownership to the quieter half of the team without lowering what is expected of them.
sessions.emergingThemes:
The advisers' suggestions were more operationally specific than her own, which Sophie noticed aloud and did not treat as a threat.

Accountability now runs through a mechanism — owner, action, date — rather than depending on whether she feels able to chase someone.

Her language has moved from 'would you mind' to 'who is taking this', and the team has not reacted badly to it.
sessions.strengthsObserved: She resisted supplying the answer in a forum she controls, and converted team suggestions into named accountability before the huddle ended.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Sophie is now competent at group accountability. The remaining edge is distribution, because the same two advisers carry most of the ownership.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Sustained behavioural change across several weeks: expectations are set publicly, followed up individually and closed with named owners.
sessions.agreedActions: Allocate the next two improvement items to advisers who have not owned anything yet, briefing them privately first
sessions.suggestedFocus: spreading ownership to the quieter half of the team without lowering what is expected of them
sessions.coachReflection: Confidence has become procedural for Sophie, which is more durable than feeling confident. The open question is whether the procedure survives a bad week.

sessions.title: Development conversation 6
sessions.preparation: Bring the outage Friday: what you did, what you wanted to do, and what the team managed without you.
sessions.notes: Reviewed the outage Friday. Sophie stayed out of the queue, delegated recovery and handled callbacks and communications. Monday debrief led with process questions. Reported feeling useless during the incident.
sessions.summary: Sophie faced a missed service level on the Friday of a systems outage, with ninety calls queuing and two advisers absent. Taking calls herself is the rescue instinct she called impossible to resist in February, and she held back on the worst operational day of the year. Sophie stayed out of the queue, asked the senior adviser to run recovery, and spent the afternoon on the customer callback list and the outage communication instead. Discomfort has not disappeared for her; it has stopped being the thing that decides what she does. She debriefed the shift on Monday by asking what the process had allowed, and the team raised two issues before she did. Sophie's judgement about where a manager adds value during a failure is sound: callbacks and communication mattered more than one extra person on the phones. She described feeling useless during the outage, so the behaviour has travelled further than the belief underneath it. The following session will test sustaining the standard through the autumn peak, when three advisers are due to leave the team. Sophie committed to write a short outage playbook with the senior adviser setting out who runs recovery and what the manager does.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Sophie's judgement about where a manager adds value during a failure is sound: callbacks and communication mattered more than one extra person on the phones.

The team's willingness to raise problems in the Monday debrief suggests the accountability she built is not experienced as blame.

Discomfort has not disappeared for her; it has stopped being the thing that decides what she does.
sessions.strengthsObserved: She held a management position during a live service failure and spent the time on work that only the manager could do.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Sophie's confidence is now visible in operational decisions. Help the belief catch up with the behaviour rather than adding new stretch.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Confidence has become behavioural: a former peer group is managed to clear standards, ownership sits with advisers, and pressure no longer reverses the pattern.
sessions.agreedActions: Write a short outage playbook with the senior adviser setting out who runs recovery and what the manager does
sessions.suggestedFocus: sustaining the standard through the autumn peak, when three advisers are due to leave the team
sessions.coachReflection: The gap between what Sophie now does and what she still feels is worth naming with her. Behaviour has led; belief follows if she keeps noticing the evidence.

sessions.title: Development conversation 1
sessions.preparation: Bring last Monday's dashboard and everything you personally decided before ten o'clock.
sessions.notes: Reviewed the Monday backlog and the pre-nine reallocation of three engineers. Mapped how supervisors are bypassed once the backlog becomes visible. No supervisor recovery plans currently requested.
sessions.summary: A field-service backlog of 240 jobs appeared on the Monday dashboard, and Marcus had reallocated three engineers before nine o'clock. He described the reallocation as obvious and necessary, then worked out during the conversation that he had spoken to none of his four supervisors before making it. Marcus intervenes fastest when a problem is visible to his director, which suggests the trigger is exposure rather than operational risk. Speed is what Marcus is rewarded for, and it is also what teaches four supervisors that the backlog belongs to him rather than to them. The pattern itself is unchanged this month. What is new is that he can trace it to one specific morning and one specific decision. There is no protected time anywhere in his week; every hour is available to whatever the dashboard shows at nine. He is not convinced the supervisors could have handled it, and that belief has not been tested against any evidence. The commitment he made was to list the decisions made last week that a supervisor could have made, and bring that list to the next conversation. The next session examines testing whether supervisor silence is a capability problem or a consequence of being overruled.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Marcus intervenes fastest when a problem is visible to his director, which suggests the trigger is exposure rather than operational risk.

Two of the four supervisors have stopped bringing him recovery plans, which he reads as a capability gap and may be a response to being overruled.

There is no protected time anywhere in his week; every hour is available to whatever the dashboard shows at nine.
sessions.strengthsObserved: Marcus knows the operation in detail and can diagnose a parts-allocation failure faster than anyone else in the function.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Marcus measures himself on response speed. Challenge will land better framed as building capacity than as stepping back from the work.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Early awareness only: the firefighting pattern has been named and dated, and connected to what his supervisors have stopped doing.
sessions.agreedActions: List the decisions made last week that a supervisor could have made, and bring that list to the next conversation
sessions.suggestedFocus: testing whether supervisor silence is a capability problem or a consequence of being overruled
sessions.coachReflection: Marcus accepts the diagnosis quickly and moves past it just as quickly. The value here is staying with the cost of the pattern long enough to want it changed.

sessions.title: One-to-one
sessions.preparation: Aurelia prompt: which of your supervisors would notice first if you stopped writing their plans, and what would they do instead?
sessions.notes: Parts shortage in the western depot. Recovery plans requested from four supervisors; three received and one weaker plan run unchanged. Missing plan not followed up. Two reversions to direct instruction later in the week.
sessions.summary: A parts shortage in the western depot left forty jobs unallocated, and Marcus asked each supervisor for a recovery plan by midday instead of issuing one himself. Asking for plans changed the depot conversation immediately: two supervisors brought parts data he had never seen. Three plans arrived. One was, in his own words, worse than what he would have written, and he ran it anyway to find out what would happen. Running the weaker plan cost half a day and produced the first evidence that the operation does not fail when he is not the author of the answer. This is a single experiment rather than a habit. He reverted to direct instruction twice later the same week when a customer escalation arrived. The fourth supervisor submitted nothing and Marcus let it pass, so the request was optional in practice. He tolerates a weaker plan while the stakes stay internal, and takes over the moment a customer name is attached to the problem. Work continues on turning the recovery plan request into a standing expectation rather than a one-off. Marcus agreed to ask the fourth supervisor directly why no plan arrived, and agree what happens the next time one is missing.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Asking for plans changed the depot conversation immediately: two supervisors brought parts data he had never seen.

He tolerates a weaker plan while the stakes stay internal, and takes over the moment a customer name is attached to the problem.

The missing plan is the more important signal of the week, and it passed without any comment at all.
sessions.strengthsObserved: He let a suboptimal plan run to completion rather than correcting it, which was the more informative choice available.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Marcus experiments willingly. It is the follow-through on non-compliance where he backs off, particularly with the longest-serving supervisor.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: A first deliberate change in practice: recovery planning was requested rather than supplied, and one plan ran unaltered.
sessions.agreedActions: Ask the fourth supervisor directly why no plan arrived, and agree what happens the next time one is missing
sessions.suggestedFocus: turning the recovery plan request into a standing expectation rather than a one-off
sessions.coachReflection: The uncomfortable material here is the missing plan, not the weak one. Marcus finds operational quality far easier to discuss than holding someone to a request.

sessions.title: Feedback conversation
sessions.preparation: Bring the two sets of actions you rewrote, alongside what the supervisors originally proposed.
sessions.notes: Weekly exception review established, chaired in rotation. Ageing jobs down from forty-one to twenty-six. Two supervisors' actions rewritten after the meeting without their knowledge. Agreed to issue actions unedited for three weeks.
sessions.summary: Marcus introduced a weekly exception review covering every job older than five days, chaired by the supervisors in rotation. The routine hands supervisors visible ownership and the rewrite quietly takes it back, so the meeting and the follow-up now teach opposite lessons. The first two meetings ran well, and afterwards he rewrote the actions of two supervisors and circulated them under his own name. The improvement in ageing jobs is genuine and gives him something to protect, which should make the next step easier to argue. The structure is real and holding. Three reviews have run and ageing jobs have fallen from forty-one to twenty-six. Marcus builds good mechanisms and then reoccupies them, which makes the mechanism look successful while the behaviour underneath stays the same. Neither supervisor knows their actions were rewritten, so both are working to a plan they never agreed. He took away one task: issue the exception review actions unedited for the next three weeks, including where he would sequence them differently. The focus ahead is leaving supervisor decisions intact long enough to see whether the outcome genuinely suffers.

Marcus builds good mechanisms and then reoccupies them, which makes the mechanism look successful while the behaviour underneath stays the same.

The improvement in ageing jobs is genuine and gives him something to protect, which should make the next step easier to argue.

His rewrites concerned sequencing rather than substance, suggesting a preference for control of method rather than any disagreement about outcome.
sessions.strengthsObserved: He designed and launched a weekly review that produced a measurable fall in ageing jobs inside three weeks.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Marcus's instinct is to improve the answer. Ask what a supervisor learns when the improved answer arrives without them in it.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Mixed evidence: a delegation structure now exists and works, while the habit of authoring the detail persists behind it.
sessions.agreedActions: Issue the exception review actions unedited for the next three weeks, including where he would sequence them differently
sessions.suggestedFocus: leaving supervisor decisions intact long enough to see whether the outcome genuinely suffers
sessions.coachReflection: The interesting question is what Marcus believes would happen if an imperfect supervisor plan reached the depot with that supervisor's name on it.

sessions.title: Performance conversation
sessions.preparation: Bring the capacity forecast, the two options you offered, and what the director did with them.
sessions.notes: Capacity forecast completed after two-hour Tuesday blocks were protected; three of four held. Two staffing options and a recommendation presented to the operations director. One block lost to an escalation already owned by a supervisor.
sessions.summary: The autumn capacity forecast, which had sat on Marcus's list since March, was finally written. He blocked two hours every Tuesday, held three of the four blocks, and took the operations director a forecast containing two staffing options and a stated recommendation. Strategic work only happened once it had a slot, a deadline and an audience; intention alone had produced nothing in five months. The director's response was that this was the first time she had been handed a choice rather than a problem, which changed what his protected time is worth. The blocks survived three ordinary weeks, and the exception review absorbed two issues that would previously have eaten straight into them. He still describes strategic work as what he does when the operation allows it, rather than as the substance of the job. The block he did lose went to a customer escalation that a supervisor had already picked up. The commitment he made was to agree a standing monthly slot with the operations director for forward capacity and cost trade-offs. The next session examines holding the protected blocks through a genuinely bad operational week.
sessions.emergingThemes:
Strategic work only happened once it had a slot, a deadline and an audience; intention alone had produced nothing in five months.

The forecast was strongest where it used depot data his supervisors had produced, which is an argument for the routine he built last month.

He still describes strategic work as what he does when the operation allows it, rather than as the substance of the job.
sessions.strengthsObserved: He turned six months of intention into a forecast with options and a recommendation, and defended that recommendation when it was questioned.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Marcus responds to external commitments. A fixed monthly slot with the director will protect this work far better than willpower.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Emerging change with real substance: strategic capacity is being protected and used, and supervisor-produced data is feeding into it.
sessions.agreedActions: Agree a standing monthly slot with the operations director for forward capacity and cost trade-offs
sessions.suggestedFocus: holding the protected blocks through a genuinely bad operational week
sessions.coachReflection: Marcus has discovered that strategic work is rewarded. Watch whether that reward competes successfully with the satisfaction of clearing the backlog himself.

sessions.title: Development review
sessions.preparation: Aurelia prompt: what did your supervisors do over that weekend that you would not have predicted in February, and what does it change?
sessions.notes: Weekend generator failure resolved by two supervisors without escalation; Marcus checked twice and did not intervene. During peak week he took back a national account escalation and ran it personally for four days.
sessions.summary: A depot generator failed over a weekend and two supervisors arranged cover between themselves, telling Marcus about it on the Monday. The pattern is now legible: Marcus delegates internal operational risk and reclaims anything carrying reputational exposure. He described that Monday briefing as unsettling and useful in equal measure, and admitted he had checked the job board twice over the weekend without intervening. Cover was arranged, jobs were recovered and the customer never knew, which is the clearest evidence so far that the operation does not require his presence. Ten days later, in the middle of peak week, he took a national account escalation off the supervisor who owned it and ran it himself for four days. He describes that takeover as necessary rather than habitual, and has not tested the judgement with the supervisor concerned. The supervisors waited until Monday to tell him, which reads as confidence rather than concealment, though he first interpreted it the other way. Work continues on keeping a named account escalation with its supervisor through the next peak period. Marcus agreed to agree with all four supervisors which escalations are theirs and which are genuinely his, and write it down.

sessions.title: Development conversation 6
sessions.preparation: Bring both events: the monthly review where you held the line and the depot failure where you did not.
sessions.notes: Monthly review held at strategic level with the twelve-month capacity picture presented. Nine days later Marcus ran dispatch personally for two days during a depot service failure. Earlier structures all survived the week.
sessions.summary: Marcus went into the monthly operations review intending to keep it strategic, nine days before a service failure at the largest depot. Keeping a monthly review at that altitude in front of his director and his peers is new, and it produced the resourcing decision that four previous reviews had avoided. In the review he presented the twelve-month capacity picture and declined to be drawn into last week's job numbers, twice redirecting the discussion back to the resourcing decision. The depot recovered faster after he stepped out than during his two days in charge, which he acknowledged without defensiveness. Nine days later, during the depot failure, he ran dispatch decisions himself for two days and slipped straight back into the firefighting the supervisors had begun to own. Progress here is uneven rather than incomplete: the strategic behaviour is established in scheduled forums and absent in unscheduled crises. He can now describe the strategic role precisely and still cannot occupy it while the operation is visibly failing. He took away one task: ask the depot supervisor what she would have done differently had he stayed out, and record her answer. The focus ahead is choosing one live incident next quarter to stay out of deliberately, with the supervisor briefed in advance.

Progress here is uneven rather than incomplete: the strategic behaviour is established in scheduled forums and absent in unscheduled crises.

The depot recovered faster after he stepped out than during his two days in charge, which he acknowledged without defensiveness.

The exception review, the protected capacity slot and the escalation agreement all survived the failure week, so the structures hold even when he does not.
sessions.strengthsObserved: He kept a strategic discussion strategic under direct pressure to make it operational, and later named his own relapse without excusing it.
sessions.valuesBecomingVisible: Do not treat the relapse as programme failure. Marcus's structures held; personal behaviour under acute exposure is the edge that remains.
sessions.professionalIdentityDevelopment: Credible strategic habits alongside a live vulnerability: scheduled leadership has changed, unscheduled crisis behaviour has not yet followed.
sessions.agreedActions: Ask the depot supervisor what she would have done differently had he stayed out, and record her answer
sessions.suggestedFocus: choosing one live incident next quarter to stay out of deliberately, with the supervisor briefed in advance
sessions.coachReflection: The honest position is that Marcus has made real strategic progress and still firefights when exposed. Naming both is more useful to him than choosing between them.

sessions.title: Development conversation 1

The analysis was correct and the paper still failed, because directors were left to work out for themselves what the finance function thought they should do. Nothing has changed in her drafting yet, but she can now say plainly that she withheld the recommendation rather than forgot it. Priya's technical credibility is not in question anywhere in this business; what is missing is a stated view attached to it. She describes stating a preference as stepping outside the finance role, and that belief is entirely intact. Her commitment for the month is to rewrite the fleet paper's opening as three sentences: the decision required, the recommendation and the principal risk. The next conversation will look at whether a recommendation can be stated without the qualifications that currently surround it.

They made two decisions during the incident that later proved wrong, said so in the debrief, and the team's confidence did not drop. Manager B's confidence no longer depends on being right, which is what made the debrief useful rather than defensive. Trust across the team is improving and will need several more months of consistency before it consolidates.
